messages.content:
Title: Diagnosis

Details: The failing test `testUnsafeDeSerialization()` illustrates a security issue when deserializing a MultiValueMap with an unsafe collection class. The test first creates a MultiValueMap with ArrayList as the collection class and verifies successful serialization and deserialization without issues. However, in the second case, it creates a MultiValueMap using String.class as the collection class, which is not a Collection and hence dangerous and incorrect. When deserializing this MultiValueMap, it should fail by throwing an UnsupportedOperationException, but in the bug report, it appears this unsafe class was accepted, demonstrating a deserialization vulnerability.

From the code snippets inspected:

- The static factory method MultiValueMap.multiValueMap(map, collectionClass) creates a new MultiValueMap instance passing it a ReflectionFactory instantiated with the provided collectionClass.
- The ReflectionFactory simply stores the class and in its create() method instantiates a new instance reflectively using clazz.newInstance().
- The MultiValueMap constructor stores the collectionFactory without any validation of the class type.
- The custom deserialization method readObject(ObjectInputStream) reads the map from the stream but performs no validation or checks on the factory or the collection class type being used.
- There is no validation that the collectionClass used in ReflectionFactory actually extends or implements Collection<V>, allowing unsafe classes like String to be passed and accepted.
- This allows an attacker providing a serialized MultiValueMap to specify an unsafe class that will be instantiated on demand during map use after deserialization.

The root cause is that the class passed to ReflectionFactory (used as the collection factory) can be any class, and no validation occurs to ensure this class is a subtype of Collection. This enables dangerous classes to be set and deserialized, which can then be exploited for arbitrary code execution exploits (in the context of the bug report mentioning InvokerTransformer and remote deserialization vulnerabilities).

Hence, the vulnerability arises from lack of input validation on the factory class argument (collectionClass) used during MultiValueMap creation and deserialization.

Next, I will suggest which methods are the best locations to fix this issue.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
